title: The public trusts scientists with AI — more than it does anyone else
abstract:
Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03578-y

Public confidence in scientists’ use of generative artificial intelligence remains high, but that trust comes with conditions.
headline: People trust scientists more than others to develop AI responsibly.
why_it_matters: As AI becomes more common in medicine and cancer care, public trust in how scientists use it matters enormously. If patients don't believe AI tools are safe and ethical, they won't use them — even if they could help. This research shows that trust exists, but scientists need to understand what conditions come with it.
key_findings: Public confidence in scientists' use of generative AI (computer programs that create text, images, or predictions) is higher than trust in AI use by government, industry, or other groups.
The high trust is not unconditional — people trust scientists more when they believe AI is being used ethically and transparently.
Trust varies depending on how AI is being applied and how clearly scientists communicate what they're doing.
The public's willingness to accept AI in science depends on clear explanation of both benefits and risks.
methods_snapshot: The researchers surveyed public opinion on trust in different groups using AI. They asked people to compare their confidence in scientists versus other institutions using generative AI for various purposes.

glossary.definition: Computer software trained to create new text, images, or predictions based on patterns in existing data.
How much people believe something is trustworthy and will work as promised.
Principles about what is right and wrong in how we treat people and use tools.
Being open and honest about how something works and why decisions are made.

ml_angle: This study examined public perception of how machine learning and AI are being used by scientists, rather than using AI itself to study cancer.
limitations: This is a survey of opinions, not a measurement of actual outcomes or safety. Public trust may not match actual competence, and trust levels could differ by country, age group, or education level — the study may not represent everyone.
